newsitem.title: USA: Moscow may back debt relief plan - Russian official.
newsitem.headline: Moscow may back debt relief plan - Russian official.

text.p: Russia is prepared to support a Paris Club initiative to write off debts of poor countries and the scheme could bring Moscow $1 billion a year, a senior Russian official said on Sunday.

But former chief debt negotiator Alexander Shokhin said all debts to the former Soviet Union of the countries involved had to be included, with interest rates calculated at the former Soviet state bank's official rate at the time the debts were built up.

Russia is not getting any money from those loans because they are not being serviced, so a restructuring scheme would provide an immediate boost to its coffers, the deputy speaker of the lower house of parliament said.
"We are prepared to look and join this favourable scheme of restructuring," he told reporters ahead of a meeting of the International Monetary Fund's policy-making Interim Committee.
The Paris Club has agreed to offer debt relief of up to 80 percent on a case-by-case basis to poor heavily-indebted countries, compared with the 67 percent currently on offer.
The plan is part of a joint initiative launched with the IMF and World Bank, which are currently holding their annual meetings in Washington.

Shokhin, deputy speaker of the lower house of parliament, said the Russian delegation, led by First Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Potanin, spelled out its position in a meeting with finance ministers and central bankers from rich industrial nations on Saturday.
Some of the countries eligible for inclusion in the scheme, particularly in Africa, borrowed heavily from the Soviet Union, often on artificially advantageous terms.
However, many of them are now unable to repay the money.

Russia inherited the former Soviet Union's debts and assets. It is close to a major rescheduling agreements with its creditors from the London and Paris Clubs and is keen to join the debt-relief process as a creditor.
"The most important thing is that it is not a request from Russia that they give the money but the inclusion of Russia in a global scheme to resolve the debt problem," Shokhin said.
He said Russia was owed some $160 billion. The current 67 percent scheme could bring Moscow an immediate inflow of $2 billion a year.
"Even if it were a lesser sum, $1 billion, that is an important source of funds,"Shokhin said.
